name: Bull semen hair mask

card.summary: A salon conditioning treatment using purified protein from bull seminal plasma, promoted for smoother, shinier, stronger-looking hair.
card.aka: bull semen hair treatment, bovine seminal plasma conditioner
card.note: Marketed by salons and a product maker; independent published studies are lacking.

quick.overview:
Bull semen hair treatments are salon conditioning masks built around a protein extracted from bull semen. Their makers say the protein coats and strengthens hair, giving a shinier, smoother finish, especially on chemically damaged hair.

The treatment drew media attention in 2007 when a London salon offered it, and a New Zealand firm, the Natural Protein Company, marketed a range called Imprivo. The company said independent tests at a Crown Research Institute found increased tensile strength in damaged hair; no peer-reviewed trial appears in the literature.
quick.how: It is applied in a salon as a conditioning treatment lasting about 45 minutes, sometimes with plant extracts. A 2007 report priced the London version at roughly 55 to 85 pounds.
quick.risks: Makers say the sperm cells are removed and only the purified seminal plasma protein is used. No safety data have been published in journals; as with any new topical product, allergic reactions are possible.

lead: The bull semen hair mask is a salon conditioning treatment that uses a protein extracted from the seminal plasma of bulls. It is promoted as a way to make hair look shinier, smoother and stronger, particularly after colouring or other damage.[1]
The product the company describes is not raw semen: the semen is centrifuged to remove sperm, and the remaining liquid is purified to extract a bio-protein.[1]
The treatment is known mostly through news and trade coverage. Evidence for its effects comes from company statements.

chain: Protein from bovine seminal plasma applied as a salon mask
Said to bind to damaged hair and raise tensile strength
Hair looks shinier and feels smoother
angle.text: Salons and the maker say the protein improves strength and shine of damaged hair, similar to other protein conditioning treatments. The claim rests on company-reported tests.

paras: The treatment is a protein-based conditioner. Makers describe the ingredient as bovine seminal plasma (BSP), purified after centrifugation, with sperm removed.[1] Salon marketing has emphasised organic, protein-rich ingredients.

In 2007 trade press reported that a London salon offered a 45-minute treatment using semen from Aberdeen Angus bulls with a plant root extract, with a stated aim of a high-protein organic product. A New Zealand company, the Natural Protein Company, later promoted the Imprivo range, trademarked in Japan and aimed at high-end salons in the UK, US and Hong Kong.[1]

The company describes the protein as anti-bacterial and nourishing, and says treated chemically damaged hair returns close to its undamaged condition. Its technical director said there is good science behind it.[1] Salon spokespeople said the proteins create a shine other treatments could not match.

The maker reports independent tensile-strength tests at a Crown Research Institute.[1] Proteins applied to hair generally act as temporary conditioning; dermatologists and trichologists have not published studies on this specific product.

timeline.event: A London salon offers a bull-semen protein conditioning treatment; trade press covers it.
New Zealand coverage describes the Imprivo range using bovine seminal plasma protein.[1]
